title: Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare Convenes National Workshop on Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK)
subtitle:
Early Identification, Risk-Based Follow-up and Timely Action Key to Improving Child Health Outcomes: Smt. Aradhana Patnaik, Additional Secretary & Mission Director, National Health Mission (NHM)
Risk-Differentiated Care to Enable Early Identification and Intensified Follow-up of ‘At-risk’ Newborns and Children & Shaishav App to Enable Digital Tracking of Children, Home Visits, Follow-up and Referrals
Workshop Focuses on Strengthening Digital Monitoring and Continuum of Care under SSBSK
body_text:
Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) convened a two-day National Workshop on Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK) on August 24–25, 2026, at Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Maharashtra. The workshop was held under the chairpersonship of Smt. Aradhana Patnaik, Additional Secretary & Mission Director, National Health Mission (NHM), MoHFW, and brought together senior officials from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India; representatives of the Government of Maharashtra; State Nodal Officers for Child Health and ASHA programme from all 36 States and Union Territories; technical experts; and development partners.
The workshop focused on translating the SSBSK Operational Guidelines into effective implementation at the State, district, health facility and community levels, with particular emphasis on strengthening the continuum of care for newborns and young children from birth to three years of age.
Delivering the keynote address, Smt. Aradhana Patnaik, Additional Secretary & Mission Director, National Health Mission, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India, emphasised that while India has made substantial progress in reducing newborn and child mortality, the remaining challenge requires greater attention to vulnerable newborns and children, particularly the first 7 days of life which are critical for newborn survival, and the first 3 years for optimal brain development underscoring SSBSK's continuum of care for every child's survival, growth and development.
She also highlighted the need to move from routine service delivery towards early identification, risk-based follow-up and timely action, with States playing a central role in translating the SSBSK framework into measurable improvements in child health outcomes. She reiterated that effective implementation will require strong teamwork between ASHAs, ANMs, Community Health Officers, Medical Officers and Anganwadi Workers, supported by effective supervision, referral linkages and programme monitoring.
The inaugural session commenced with the welcome address by Dr. Shobhna Gupta, Deputy Commissioner & In-charge (Child Health & RBSK), Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, who set the context for the two-day national workshop and underscored the importance of coordinated and convergent action among stakeholders for effective implementation of SSBSK.
Sharing the State of Maharashtra's perspective on newborn and child health survival, Shri Sanjay Shripatrao Katkar, Commissioner & Mission Director (NHM), Government of Maharashtra, highlighted the importance of strong State leadership and health-system action in advancing newborn and child survival and translating national programme priorities into implementation at the field level.
Development partners also addressed the gathering, including Dr Hemang Shah, Director (CIFF), Health & Nutrition, India; Dr Pushpa Deo Chaudhary, Team Lead (RMNCAH), WHO India; Ms Nande Putta, Chief of Health, UNICEF India; and Mr Arvinn Gadgil, Deputy Ambassador of Norway to India, reaffirming their support for strengthening newborn and child health services and implementation of SSBSK.
During the inaugural session, SSBSK programme resources were released, including the SSBSK inauguration video, the Shaishav App video and SSBSK training videos for frontline workers, to support programme communication, orientation and capacity building.
A key focus of the workshop was the Shaishav App, the digital platform supporting SSBSK implementation. The application is designed to enable identification and digital line-listing of ‘At-risk’ newborns and children, scheduling and tracking of home visits, follow-up of referrals, supportive supervision and programme monitoring. The digital platform will support the creation of a longitudinal child health profile, enabling continuity of information and follow-up as a child progresses from the newborn period through early childhood. The emphasis is on using technology as an enabler for timely decision-making while ensuring that compassionate, family-centred care remains at the heart of programme delivery.
The workshop also highlighted the importance of strengthening follow-up through community and primary healthcare platforms, including VHSNDs, Ayushman Arogya Mandir–Sub Centres and other child health service delivery platforms, to ensure that children identified with health, nutrition, growth or developmental concerns do not get lost to follow-up.
Dedicated technical sessions during the workshop covered the key components of SSBSK, including risk identification and differentiated care; home-visit schedules; maternal postnatal and mental health; infant and young child feeding; growth and developmental monitoring; nurturing care and early childhood development; identification of danger signs; referral and follow-up; joint home visits; supportive supervision; and use of the Shaishav App.
Special emphasis was placed on the role of families in nurturing care. Participants discussed the importance of engaging mothers, fathers, grandparents and other family members in responsive caregiving, age-appropriate play and communication, appropriate feeding practices and early recognition of health and developmental concerns.
The group work conducted with all participants to discuss implementation preparedness, operational challenges, training and capacity-building requirements, convergence mechanisms and State-specific implementation strategies. The deliberations reinforced the importance of States as active partners and co-owners of SSBSK implementation.
About Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK)
The Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK), launched by Union Minister for Health and Family Welfare Shri J.P. Nadda on 29 June 2026 during the 16th Conference of the Central Council of Health and Family Welfare (CCHFW), marks a significant shift in India’s approach to newborn and young child health. Integrating HBNC and HBYC into a unified, risk-stratified and digitally enabled continuum of home- and community-based care from birth to 36 months, under the vision “पहले तीन साल, सम्पूर्ण देखभाल,” the programme goes beyond child survival to focus on healthy growth and development, nutrition, nurturing care, maternal well-being, early identification of illness and developmental concerns, and timely referral and follow-up.
A key feature of SSBSK is risk-differentiated care, under which ‘At-risk’ newborns and children receive intensified follow-up, additional home visits, closer monitoring and strengthened referral support. The programme also provides for joint home visits by frontline health workers and primary healthcare teams for ‘At-risk’ children, enabling coordinated assessment, strengthened clinical oversight and counselling, and better continuity between home-based care and health facilities.

ministry.name: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

enrichment.summary: The Union Health Ministry held a two-day National Workshop (24-25 August 2026) at Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Maharashtra, on the Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK), chaired by NHM Mission Director Aradhana Patnaik. The workshop focused on operationalising SSBSK's risk-differentiated care model and the 'Shaishav App', a digital platform for tracking 'at-risk' newborns and children, home visits, referrals and follow-up. State nodal officers from all 36 States/UTs, technical experts and development partners (WHO, UNICEF, CIFF, Norway) participated to discuss implementation strategies for the continuum of care from birth to three years.
enrichment.context:
SSBSK was launched by Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda on 29 June 2026 during the 16th Conference of the Central Council of Health and Family Welfare, merging two existing home-based care schemes—Home Based Newborn Care (HBNC) and Home Based Care for Young Child (HBYC)—into a single, risk-stratified, digitally enabled programme covering the first 36 months of life. Its slogan, 'पहले तीन साल, सम्पूर्ण देखभाल' (First three years, complete care), reflects a shift in India's child health strategy from a narrow survival focus to comprehensive growth, nutrition, nurturing care, maternal wellbeing and developmental monitoring, executed through ASHAs, ANMs, Community Health Officers and Anganwadi Workers.

This workshop is significant because it marks the first major national-level exercise to translate SSBSK's operational guidelines into field-level practice, less than two months after launch, and introduces the Shaishav App as the digital backbone for maintaining longitudinal child health profiles. Such convergence of home-based care, primary health infrastructure (Ayushman Arogya Mandir-Sub Centres, VHSNDs) and digital monitoring reflects broader trends in India's health governance—integrating fragmented vertical schemes and leveraging technology for real-time tracking, similar to efforts like POSHAN Tracker and RCH portal in maternal-child health governance.

prelims_questions.question: The Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK) integrates which two existing schemes into a unified continuum of care?
options: Janani Suraksha Yojana and Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram
Home Based Newborn Care (HBNC) and Home Based Care for Young Child (HBYC)
Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram and Mission Indradhanush
Integrated Child Development Services and POSHAN Abhiyaan
prelims_questions.explanation: As stated in the release, SSBSK integrates HBNC and HBYC into a unified, risk-stratified and digitally enabled continuum of home- and community-based care from birth to 36 months.

prelims_questions.question: The 'Shaishav App', mentioned in connection with SSBSK, is primarily designed to:
options: Provide telemedicine consultations to pregnant women
Enable digital identification, tracking of home visits, and follow-up/referral of at-risk newborns and children
Disburse maternity benefit cash transfers under PMMVY
Track immunization coverage under Mission Indradhanush
prelims_questions.explanation: The release describes the Shaishav App as a digital platform enabling identification and line-listing of 'at-risk' newborns and children, scheduling of home visits, and follow-up of referrals under SSBSK.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of a risk-differentiated, continuum-of-care approach in improving newborn and child health outcomes in India. How does the Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK) attempt to operationalise this approach?
Examine the role of digital platforms in strengthening last-mile delivery of maternal and child health services in India, with reference to recent initiatives such as the Shaishav App under SSBSK.

study_notes.reason: SSBSK carries a testable factual core (merger of HBNC/HBYC, launch date, risk-differentiated care model, Shaishav App features, 36-month continuum) and genuine analytical depth on India's shift from survival-focused to comprehensive child health governance, digital integration and last-mile convergence challenges.

prelims.point: SSBSK merges two earlier home-based care schemes: Home Based Newborn Care (HBNC) and Home Based Care for Young Child (HBYC)
prelims.why_important: UPSC frequently tests scheme mergers/rebranding and their constituent predecessor programmes; distinguishing HBNC/HBYC from SSBSK is a classic prelims trap.

prelims.point: SSBSK was launched by Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda on 29 June 2026 during the 16th Conference of the Central Council of Health and Family Welfare (CCHFW)
prelims.why_important: Launch date, forum and minister are typical factual pegs for scheme-identification questions.

prelims.point: SSBSK covers the continuum of care from birth to 36 months (three years) of age
prelims.why_important: The specific age bracket distinguishes SSBSK from other child health schemes like RBSK (which covers 0-18 years) and is a likely distinguishing fact in objective questions.

prelims.point: 'Shaishav App' is the digital platform under SSBSK for line-listing 'At-risk' newborns/children, tracking home visits, referrals and creating a longitudinal child health profile
prelims.why_important: Naming and function of programme-specific digital tools is a recurring prelims theme, similar to POSHAN Tracker or RCH portal questions.

prelims.point: SSBSK is implemented under the National Health Mission (NHM), with State Nodal Officers for Child Health and ASHA programme coordinating across all 36 States/UTs
prelims.why_important: Institutional architecture (NHM as umbrella, nodal officer structure) is testable in questions on health governance frameworks.

prelims.point: SSBSK's slogan is 'पहले तीन साल, सम्पूर्ण देखभाल' (First three years, complete care)
prelims.why_important: Scheme slogans are occasionally used as identifiers in prelims matching questions.

mains.point: SSBSK reflects a strategic shift in India's child health policy from a narrow survival focus to comprehensive growth, nutrition, nurturing care and developmental monitoring
mains.analytical_use: Useful for 'Discuss/Examine' questions on the evolution of India's maternal-child health strategy and how survival-centric approaches are being replaced by holistic developmental frameworks.

mains.point: Risk-differentiated care model enables targeted, intensified follow-up for 'at-risk' newborns/children rather than uniform service delivery
mains.analytical_use: Can be deployed in questions on efficient resource allocation in public health, evaluating shift from universal to risk-stratified interventions.

mains.point: Integration of digital tools (Shaishav App) with community health platforms (VHSNDs, Ayushman Arogya Mandir-Sub Centres) exemplifies convergence of technology and grassroots health infrastructure
mains.analytical_use: Relevant for questions on role of digital technology in strengthening last-mile health service delivery and reducing children 'lost to follow-up'.

mains.point: Effective implementation depends on inter-cadre teamwork among ASHAs, ANMs, Community Health Officers, Medical Officers and Anganwadi Workers
mains.analytical_use: Supports 'way forward' sections in answers on implementation challenges of health schemes reliant on multi-cadre frontline convergence.

mains.point: Merging of vertical schemes (HBNC, HBYC) into one unified programme signals broader trend of integrating fragmented health schemes for better outcomes
mains.analytical_use: Can be cited as an example while analysing challenges of scheme fragmentation and the case for consolidation in India's welfare architecture.

mains.point: Engagement of development partners (WHO, UNICEF, CIFF, Norway) highlights the role of international cooperation in strengthening domestic health programmes
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on the role of multilateral/bilateral partners in supporting India's public health goals.

both.concept: Shaishav App as digital backbone for risk-differentiated care
both.prelims_angle: Name, purpose and functions of the app (line-listing, home-visit tracking, referral follow-up, longitudinal profile) can be tested as a factual identifier.
both.mains_angle: Its role illustrates how digital tools can operationalise risk-based public health interventions and prevent children from being 'lost to follow-up', a recurring governance challenge in India's health delivery.
